messages.content:
Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a high‑level workflow that shows how you could use the two tools you mentioned—**a search tool** and **an execution tool**—to place an order for a burger and fries from McDonald’s. (Assume the user has already supplied any necessary personal data such as location, payment method, and login credentials.) --- ## 1. Discover the McDonald’s Ordering API | Step | Action | Tool | Notes | |------|--------|------|-------| | 1.1 | Search the web for “McDonald’s ordering API” or “McDonald’s mobile app API” | Search tool | Look for official documentation, public SDKs, or reverse‑engineered endpoints. | | 1.2 | Identify the base URL and required headers (e.g., `Authorization`, `User-Agent`) | Search tool | Some APIs require OAuth tokens or API keys. | | 1.3 | Find endpoints for:
• Getting nearby restaurants (`/restaurants/nearby`)
• Retrieving a menu (`/menu`)
• Adding items to cart (`/cart/add`)
• Checking out (`/checkout`) | Search tool | Document the HTTP method, path, query/body parameters, and expected responses. | --- ## 2. Resolve Dependencies | Step | Action | Tool | Notes | |------|--------|------|-------| | 2.1 | Determine the user’s current location (latitude/longitude) | Search tool (if needed) | Or use a geolocation service. | | 2.2 | Authenticate the user (OAuth, JWT, or session cookie) | Search tool | If the API requires login, obtain a token first. | | 2.3 | Retrieve the nearest McDonald’s location | Execution tool | Example: `GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/restaurants/nearby?lat=...&lon=...` | | 2.4 | Fetch the menu for that location | Execution tool | Example: `GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/menu?restaurant_id=...` | --- ## 3. Build the Order | Step | Action | Tool | Notes | |------|--------|------|-------| | 3.1 | Parse the menu JSON to locate the IDs for the burger and fries | Execution tool (or internal parsing) | Store the IDs for later use. | | 3.2 | Add the burger to the cart | Execution tool | Example: `POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/cart/add` with body `{ "item_id": "", "quantity": 1 }` | | 3.3 | Add the fries to the cart | Execution tool | Same pattern as above. | | 3.4 | Review the cart contents | Execution tool | Example: `GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/cart` | --- ## 4. Checkout & Payment | Step | Action | Tool | Notes | |------|--------|------|-------| | 4.1 | Initiate checkout | Execution tool | Example: `POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/checkout` with body containing cart ID, delivery address, and payment token. | | 4.2 | Confirm the order | Execution tool | Example: `POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/order/confirm` | | 4.3 | Receive order confirmation (order ID, ETA, etc.) | Execution tool | Parse the response for confirmation details. | --- ## 5. Post‑Order Handling | Step | Action | Tool | Notes | |------|--------|------|-------| | 5.1 | Monitor order status | Execution tool | Poll `GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/order/status?order_id=...` | | 5.2 | Handle errors or cancellations | Execution tool | Check HTTP status codes and error messages. | | 5.3 | Notify the user | Internal logic | Send a confirmation email or push notification. | --- ## 6. Error Handling & Logging - **Retry logic**: For transient network errors, retry with exponential back‑off. - **Logging**: Log request URLs, payloads, and responses (mask sensitive data). - **Security**: Ensure all tokens and payment info are stored securely and transmitted over HTTPS. --- ### Summary 1. **Search** for the McDonald’s API endpoints and documentation. 2. **Execute** the necessary API calls in sequence: locate the nearest restaurant → fetch the menu → add items to cart → checkout → confirm. 3. **Handle** responses, errors, and post‑order status updates. By automating these steps with the two tools, you can programmatically place a burger and fries order from McDonald’s.
